e.etymology: A respelling of Ashton, an English surname and place name from Old English aesc (ash tree) plus tun (settlement). With the -yn ending it is given to girls about as often as boys.

e.meaning: of the Julius family; traditionally read as youthful
e.etymology: The Italian form of Julia, the feminine of the Roman family name Julius. It has been one of the most popular girls' names in Italy for decades.

assoc.t: Alfa Romeo Giulia, Italian sports sedan

e.etymology: A spelling used mainly by Indian families. It matches Ivan, the Slavic form of John (God is gracious), with the doubled a of Vihaan and Ayaan. Indian name lists gloss it as sun or ruler, without a clear source.
Borrowed in the 18th century from German Ernst, a medieval royal name from Old High German ernust (vigor, strife). Oscar Wilde's comedy The Importance of Being Earnest plays on its sound.
namesakes: Ernest Hemingway (novelist)
Ernest Shackleton (Antarctic explorer)
Ernest P. Worrell (Jim Varney's comedy character)

assoc.t: Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest, a pun on the name
Ernest P. Worrell of the Ernest comedies

e.etymology: A 20th-century American coinage, a spelling of Jaylynn, which joins Jay to the -lyn ending of Kaitlyn and Brooklyn.
The French form of Adrian, from Latin Hadrianus, a man from Hadria, the town in northern Italy that also named the Adriatic Sea. The Roman emperor Hadrian bore the same name.
namesakes: Adrien Brody (Oscar-winning actor, The Pianist)
Adrien Agreste (Cat Noir in the cartoon Miraculous)

assoc.t: Adrien Agreste, Cat Noir in the cartoon Miraculous

e.etymology: From Sanskrit rishi (sage, seer), the word for the inspired poets to whom the hymns of the Vedas are credited.
namesakes: Rishi Sunak (British prime minister, 2022 to 2024)

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Alicia, a Latinized form of Alice, which goes back to the Germanic name Adalheidis (noble kind).
The English word, from Latin patientia (endurance), adopted as a virtue name by the Puritans in the 16th and 17th centuries.

assoc.t: Patience, the Guns N' Roses ballad
patience, the British name for solitaire

e.etymology: A spelling of Alison, a medieval Norman French pet form of Alice. Alice goes back to the Germanic name Adalheidis (noble kind).
namesakes: Alyson Hannigan (Buffy and How I Met Your Mother actress)
Alyson Stoner (actor and dancer, Camp Rock)

e.etymology: A Swiss and German form of Nikolaus, from Greek Nikolaos: nike (victory) plus laos (people). It is the same name as Nicholas.
namesakes: Niklaus Mikaelson (Klaus, an original vampire in The Vampire Diaries and The Originals)

assoc.t: Klaus Mikaelson's full first name in The Originals

e.etymology: The Czech and Slavic feminine of Jan (John), from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. A separate Arabic name spelled the same way means harvest or fruit.
namesakes: Jana Kramer (country singer and One Tree Hill actress)

e.etymology: A Turkish name traced to Greek Helene, the source of Helen. In the US it also works as a spelling of Alayna.
An English surname for someone who lived in a slade, from Old English slaed, a small valley or dell.

assoc.t: DC Comics villain Deathstroke (Slade Wilson) in Teen Titans

e.etymology: A Dutch short form of Coenraad (Conrad), from Germanic words for bold and counsel. In the US it is also used as a spelling of the surname Cohen, Hebrew for priest.

assoc.t: the Coen brothers, filmmakers of Fargo

e.note: Sounds the same as Cohen, a Jewish priestly title; some Jewish people object to its use as a first name.

e.etymology: Popularized by the heroine of Nickelodeon's The Legend of Korra (2012); American use as a baby name took off with the show. It echoes the older name Cora.
namesakes: Korra (the Avatar in Nickelodeon's The Legend of Korra)

assoc.t: Avatar Korra, heroine of The Legend of Korra

e.meaning: lovable; often read as beautiful Anna
e.etymology: A form of Annabel, which began in medieval Scotland as an alteration of Amabel, from Latin amabilis (lovable). It was later reinterpreted as Anna plus bella, beautiful.
namesakes: Annabella Sciorra (actress in The Sopranos and Jungle Fever)

e.etymology: A respelling of Zoe, from Greek zoe, life. Zoe was used in Greek as a translation of Eve.
A recent American coinage that joins Cash to the -ton ending of names like Ashton and Paxton.
The Scandinavian and Finnish form of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el, a rhetorical question meaning who is like God? Michael is the archangel who leads heaven's armies.
namesakes: Mikael Blomkvist (journalist hero of The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo)

e.etymology: The English word, from Latin divinus, belonging to a god. It is used as a given name in the US and in English-speaking West Africa.

assoc.t: drag performer Divine, star of John Waters films

e.etymology: From Hebrew Ya'ir, he will light up, the name of a judge of Israel in the Bible. It is now most common in Latin America, alongside Jairo and Yahir.
namesakes: Jair Bolsonaro (former president of Brazil)

e.etymology: From Arabic kamila, the feminine of Kamil, perfect or complete. In the US the spelling also overlaps with Camila and Kamila.
The Spanish, Portuguese and Latin word for love. Amor is also a Latin name for Cupid, the god of love.

assoc.t: Spanish word for love, familiar from song lyrics
Latin name for Cupid, Roman god of love

e.etymology: A spelling of Mason, the occupational surname for a stoneworker. The spelling matches the French word maison, house.

assoc.t: French word for house, used in fashion-house names

e.note: Maison is the French word for house, so some people will read it as may-ZOHN.

e.meaning: dear, beloved; also friend in Irish
e.etymology: A 20th-century English coinage from Italian cara, dear, or Irish cara, friend. It was not a traditional name in Italy or Ireland.
namesakes: Cara Delevingne (model and actress)

e.etymology: From Latin patricia, the feminine of patricius, a member of the Roman nobility. It later came to be seen as the feminine of Patrick.
namesakes: Patricia Arquette (Oscar-winning actress in Boyhood)
Patricia Heaton (actress in Everybody Loves Raymond)
Patricia Highsmith (author of The Talented Mr. Ripley)

e.etymology: From Classical Nahuatl xochitl, flower. It has been a name among Nahuatl speakers in Mexico for centuries and is used by Mexican American families.
namesakes: Xochitl Gomez (actress, America Chavez in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness)
e.note: Most English speakers will not know how to say or spell it; expect to explain it often.

e.etymology: From Germanic ger (spear) plus wald (rule, power). The Normans brought it to England; it survived in Ireland and was revived in the 19th century.
namesakes: Gerald Ford (38th US president)

assoc.t: Gerald the elephant in Mo Willems' Elephant & Piggie books

e.etymology: From the Welsh surname Vaughan, from bychan, small or junior, a byname for the younger of two men with the same name.
In US use since the 1970s, mainly in Black families. Its source is unclear; it is often linked to the East African name Ayana.
namesakes: Ayanna Pressley (US congresswoman from Massachusetts)

e.etymology: The French form of Julius, a Roman family name of uncertain meaning. In English it is also a short form of Julian, Julia and Julie, which is how girls come to share it.
namesakes: Jules Verne (author of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea)
Jules Winnfield (Samuel L. Jackson's hitman in Pulp Fiction)
